Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Reuters US-Israel war on Iran Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 31 Aug 2026 13.13 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates in response. The US president, Donald Trump , on Monday threatened further action. The US is to trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. Washington claimed that Iranian control over the waterway had been loosened by repeated US attacks on Iranian missile launchers and radars. US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday, launching the first strikes on Iran since July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the strait. Last week Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies. In response to the US attack, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”. The UAE defence ministry said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters. Trump responded to the Iranian reprisals by telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” The US president called Iran “officially a failed nation without an airforce, a navy or a currency”, adding that inflation was at 300% and its leaders were incapable of representing their country. Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaign Read more The White House last week signalled that Trump was shelving military measures in favour of a campaign to destroy the Iranian economy by enforcing sanctions . Iranian state TV claimed the military exchanges escalated on Sunday after a tanker caught fire when hitting two Iranian naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. Officials later said Iran had targeted three ships trying to navigate the southern route that Tehran says is unauthorised. The IRGC warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory. However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, told Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, in a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday that continuing the war was not in Iran’s interest, adding he was still ready to implement the memorandum of understanding with the US that Pakistan had mediated in June. The Iranian currency was under renewed pressure on Monday and the inflationary impact of its rapid depreciation is causing growing concern to MPs. View image in fullscreen People buy bread from a street vendor beneath an anti-US billboard in Tehran. Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Iran and Oman last week reached a verbal agreement on a new single temporary route for shipping through the strait in which Oman retains controls on shipping in Omani waters. One western diplomat familiar with the talks said the message had got through to Washington that this bilateral agreement would not be enough for Iran to open the strait and that to do so would at least require the US to end its blockade of Iranian oil exports, something Trump is not currently prepared to do. “There are many in Iran determined to torment Trump right up to the end of his presidency,” the western diplomat said. “We are stuck.” He said some oil was getting through but not very much. The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with the US claiming it attacked Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.” The IRGC said the US attack had killed three soldiers and wounded two citizens. Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters. How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualised Read more The US said all missiles fired towards US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact. The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8m.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time. A meeting of G20 finance ministers in the US is likely to lead to a clash over American demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by Washington. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, who is facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, echoing Trump, claimed on Monday the resumed exchanges of fire showed Iran was “lashing out” because the fresh sanctions were taking ​a heavy toll on its already battered economy. View image in fullscreen Scott Bessent speaks to reporters as he arrives for the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. Photograph: Allison Joyce/AFP/Getty Images “They’re taking it very seriously ... they’re in shock at the state of their ‌economy,” Bessent told reporters at the G20 finance ministers ‌meeting in North Carolina. “I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically.” China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign. In Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete assurances from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, that he will not allow the US to spread economic chaos through Iran. https://www.dw.com/en/japanese-journalis.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OG60 A journalist for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was arrested by Russia's FSB Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Japan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Russia's ambassador after a Japanese journalist was arrested by Russia's FSB security agency on suspicion of espionage. What do know so far? The journalist's arrest comes amid a dispute in a dispute between Russia and Japan over the four southernmost islands of the Kuril Island chain, which are controlled by Moscow and claimed by Tokyo. The archipelago in the northwest Pacific is near the Russian island of Sakhalin where the man was arrested. Russia's Federal Security Service announced the arrest on Tuesday and claimed the journalist, who works for the northern Japanese Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was gathering information about Russian defense capability on behalf of Japanese intelligence. In a statement, Japan's Foreign Ministry lodged a "strong protest" against Russia for "detaining this Japanese national and issuing unilateral statements regarding the matter, while the Japanese government has not received any explanation concerning the detained national as yet." On Wednesday, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Tokyo called for Russia to treat the detainee fairly and humanely, while asking Russian authorities for more information about his arrest. Kihara added that Japanese officials have been unable to contact the man, his condition is unknown, and Moscow had not responded to Tokyo's requests for access. "We'll do everything we can for the protection of the Japanese citizen," he said. Russia claims Japan using journalists as spies Russian authorities identified the journalist as Yuki Imai. The Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper has not yet confirmed the journalist's identity, saying it is still gathering details of what could have led to the arrest. The newspaper said the man had been reporting in Russia on a journalist visa and was supposed to leave on Monday. In footage on Russian state television, a man is seen being placed in handcuffs by three masked men in black uniforms, and then being accompanied by FSB agents onto a plane. The man is then seen in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for two months. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova claimed that Japan is using accredited journalists in Russia to gather sensitive security information. Kimitake Nakamura, head of the European Affairs Bureau at Japan's Foreign Ministry, said he has asked Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to quickly arrange a meeting between the detained journalist and the Japanese government. Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Japan-Russia Kuril Islands dispute The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities. Bilateral tensions were aggravated by Japan joining Western sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine . The dispute reignited in August after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the Kurils for the first time, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling the visit "absolutely unacceptable." Putin was only the second Russian leader to ever visit the islands Russia has also increased its military presence on the islands in recent years, including by deploying missile systems, expanding air fields, and using the islands for live fire drills. In Wednesday's Foreign Ministry statement, Nakamura reiterated Japan's territorial claims over the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which Tokyo calls the "Northern Territory." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqr7yz.text: Watch: What does Starlink have to do with the Ukraine-Russia war? Watch: What does Starlink have to do with the Ukraine-Russia war? Close Ukraine says there has been a restriction to the speed of SpaceX's Starlink internet network in the country. Starlink - owned by Elon Musk - plays a vital part in the war between Ukraine and Russia, allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect itself. Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind the restriction on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connect to the network. The BBC's Dan Johnson explores who has said what in the row and how the situation affects the war.
